revealWordProblem.title: Apply: A Game of Golf
revealWordProblem.text: Golf scores are measured as strokes over or under par. Par is the number of golf strokes considered necessary to get the ball in the hole, so a score under par is written as a negative integer and a score over par is written as a positive integer. The scorecard shows six players' scores relative to par after seven holes of a 9-hole round (par = 35): Evelyn -2, Brielle +1, Terrance 0, Reginald -3, Sofia +4, Francisco +2. Order the six scores from least to greatest to rank the players from first place (the current leader) to last place. Who is winning after 7 holes, and who has the most strokes to make up?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: From least to greatest, the scores are -3, -2, 0, +1, +2, +4, which ranks the players Reginald, Evelyn, Terrance, Brielle, Francisco, Sofia. Reginald is winning after 7 holes because -3 is the least score — it is farthest left on the number line, meaning he used the fewest strokes compared to par. Sofia is in last place because +4 is the greatest score, farthest right on the number line, meaning she has used the most strokes over par.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 9.1–9.3: 9.1 Graph on the Coordinate Plane, 9.2 Integers and Absolute Value, 9.3 Compare and Order Integers. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 9.1–9.3
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 9.1: Always start at the origin (0, 0), move right/left first, then up/down. • 9.2: Absolute value tells you the distance from zero, so it is always positive or zero. • 9.3: The number farther to the left is always less; the number farther to the right is always greater.

Lesson 9.3 — Compare and Order Integers: The number farther to the left is always less; the number farther to the right is always greater.

discourse.sentenceFrame: On the number line, ___ is to the left of ___, so ___ < ___. The order from least to greatest is ___.

diagram.intro: Drag both points to compare integers. The one farther right is greater — even when a more-negative number is farther from zero.

optional.stem: (Lesson 9.1) Spot 1 — Captain Vega's first clue says the Sandy Dock is right 7 and up 2 from the origin. Which ordered pair names the Sandy Dock?
optional.explanation: The x-coordinate is the sideways move (right 7) and the y-coordinate is the up move (up 2), so the Sandy Dock is (7, 2).
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.

optional.stem: (Lesson 9.2) On a frosty morning at the mountain cache, the thermometer reads -8 degrees. What is the absolute value of -8?
optional.explanation: Absolute value is the distance from zero, so |-8| = 8.
choiceFeedback: Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.

optional.stem: (Lesson 9.3) Four spots: -3 m, 2 m, -7 m, 0 m. Order them from least to greatest.
optional.explanation: The deepest spot is the cave at -7 (farthest left), then the tide pool -3, then the boat deck 0, then the flag at 2. Least to greatest: -7, -3, 0, 2.
choiceFeedback: With negative numbers, the one farther from zero is smaller—-7 is less than -3.
Start at the left (least/smallest) on the number line and move right to the greatest.
Zero is between all negatives and all positives—check its position in your order.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.1) Which ordered pair names a point 3 units right and 7 units up from the origin?
approaching.explanation: The first coordinate is horizontal (right 3), the second is vertical (up 7). So (3, 7).
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.
hints: Re-read the moves: 3 units right, then 7 units up. Which move comes first in an ordered pair?
An ordered pair is (x, y): x is the right/left distance, y is the up/down distance. Match each move to its slot.
Start at the origin and go right 3 — that 3 is the x, the first number. Now decide where the 'up 7' goes.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.1) What are the coordinates of the origin?
approaching.explanation: The origin is where the x-axis and y-axis cross, at (0, 0).
choiceFeedback: The origin is where both axes cross, where both values are zero.
Both coordinates at the origin are 0 — not mixed with 1.
Check both the x and y values at the origin.
hints: The origin is the exact spot where the x-axis and y-axis cross. Picture that crossing point.
Ask: how far right have you moved at the origin? How far up? Those two distances are the coordinates.
At the crossing point you haven't moved right at all, so x = 0. Now figure out the y-value the same way.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.2) What is the absolute value of -9?
approaching.explanation: Absolute value is the distance from zero. -9 is 9 units from zero, so |-9| = 9.
choiceFeedback: Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: Absolute value asks: how FAR is -9 from zero? It's about distance, not direction.
Picture -9 on a number line and count the hops back to 0. A distance is never negative.
Start at -9 and count the steps to reach 0: 1, 2, 3, ... How many hops does it take in all?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.2) Which integer has the GREATEST absolute value: -3, 7, -5, 2?
choiceFeedback: Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: 'Greatest absolute value' means farthest from zero — the sign doesn't matter.
Find each number's distance from 0: |-3|, |7|, |-5|, |2|. Then pick the biggest distance.
Start with |-3| = 3 and |-5| = 5. Now find the distances for 7 and 2 and compare all four.

approaching.explanation: -5 is farther to the left on the number line than -2, so -5 < -2 is true.
choiceFeedback: With negatives, the one farther from zero is less, even though 3 > 1.
Any negative number is less than any positive number—not greater than zero.
Check on the number line: -1 is closer to zero than -6, so -1 > -6.
hints: Sketch a quick number line. For negatives, 'greater' means closer to zero, not a bigger digit.
For each statement, place both numbers on the number line: the one farther LEFT is less. Test all four.
First statement: put -3 and -1 on the line. -3 is farther left, so is '-3 > -1' true or false? Keep testing.

approaching.explanation: -8 is farthest to the left on the number line, making it the least (smallest) integer.
choiceFeedback: The least is the one farthest left on the number line—-8 is farther left than -3.
Any positive or zero is greater than any negative number.
Any positive number is greater than any negative number—check the signs.
hints: 'Least' means farthest LEFT on the number line — for negatives, that's the one farthest below zero.
Place all five numbers on a mental number line. Negatives sit left of 0, and the least is the leftmost one.
Compare just the negatives first, -3 and -8: which is farther below zero? Then check it against 0, 2, and 5.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 9.1) Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Move right
workedExample.work: Move 4 units to the right along the x-axis. Good.

workedExample.label: Move up
workedExample.work: Move 4 units up, because the pair has a 4 in it.

onLevel.correctWork: The y-coordinate is 0, not 4. After moving 4 right, the up move is 0 units, so the point stays on the x-axis at (4, 0). The student reused the x-value instead of reading the second number (0).
hints: What is the SECOND number in (4, 0), and how far up does it tell you to move?
A y-coordinate of 0 means do not move up at all — the point sits right on the x-axis at (4, 0).

onLevel.label: (Lesson 9.1) Plot these points to reveal a hidden shape: (1, 1), (1, 5), (6, 5), (6, 1)
onLevel.hint: Start at the origin (0, 0) for each point. Move right first, then up.
hints: Each pair is (x, y). For point A(1, 1) both moves are just 1 unit.
For every point: start at (0, 0), slide right x units along the bottom, then climb up y units.
Plot A first: right 1, up 1. Then B(1, 5): same x, so it sits straight above A — count up to 5.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 9.2) Which statement about absolute value is TRUE?
choices: |-4| = |4| because both are 4 units from zero
onLevel.explanation: Absolute value measures distance from zero. Both -4 and 4 are 4 units from zero, so |-4| = |4| = 4.
choiceFeedback: Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: Remember the definition: absolute value measures DISTANCE from zero, and a distance is never negative.
Test each statement against the definition. Ask: how far is -4 from zero? How far is 4? Can distance be negative?
First count -4's units from zero, then count 4's units from zero. Compare the two counts before judging.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 9.2) Confusing Opposite with Absolute Value

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: Complete the table for the integer 9: find its absolute value and its opposite.

workedExample.label: Student's thinking
workedExample.work: Absolute value and opposite both just make a number positive, so they should give the same answer as each other.

workedExample.label: Student's answer
workedExample.work: Absolute value of 9 = 9, and opposite of 9 = 9.

onLevel.correctWork: Absolute value and opposite are different operations. Absolute value measures distance from zero and is never negative: |9| = 9. Opposite reflects a number to the other side of zero, flipping its sign: the opposite of 9 is -9, not 9. The two operations only give the same result for the number 0 — every other number has a different absolute value and opposite.
hints: The opposite of a number always lands on the OTHER side of zero. Where is -9 compared to 9 on the number line?
Check the fill-table row for 4: its absolute value is 4, but its opposite is -4 — they are different! Now check the row for 9. Does the opposite of a positive number stay positive?

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 9.3) Three cities have temperatures of -12°F, -5°F, and 3°F. Which city is warmest?
onLevel.explanation: 3°F is the greatest because it is farthest to the right on the number line. The order from coldest to warmest is -12, -5, 3.
choiceFeedback: Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: Warmest = greatest temperature. On a thermometer, greater is higher — farther right on a number line.
Compare positions on a number line: temperatures farther right are warmer. Check where negatives sit versus positives.
Place -12, -5, and 3 on a number line and find the one farthest to the right. That city is warmest.

onLevel.title: (Lesson 9.3) Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Read
workedExample.work: Order -8 and -15 from least to greatest.

workedExample.label: Attempt
workedExample.work: The student wrote -8, -15, because 8 is smaller than 15.

workedExample.label: Check
workedExample.work: -15 is farther left than -8 on the number line, so -15 is the least. The correct order is -15, -8.

onLevel.correctWork: Least to greatest: -15, -8. The more negative a number is, the less its value — so -15 < -8.
hints: Which number is farther to the left on the number line?
For negative numbers, a bigger digit can mean a smaller value.

extending.title: (Lesson 9.1) Miscounted Grid Lines

workedExample.label: Move along the x-axis
workedExample.work: Start at the origin (0, 0) and count 7 units to the right.

workedExample.label: Move along the y-axis
workedExample.work: Count up from the x-axis: 1, 2, 3, 4 — stop on 4.

extending.correctWork: The x-axis itself is 0, not 1. Counting up correctly: 1, 2, 3 — the third count lands on y = 3, so the point is (7, 3), not (7, 4). The student started counting one gridline too high by treating the x-axis as unit 1 instead of unit 0.
hints: When you count up from the x-axis, is the x-axis itself unit 0 or unit 1?
The x-axis is 0. The first line above it is 1, the second is 2, the third is 3. So 3 units up lands on y = 3, not y = 4.

extending.title: (Lesson 9.2) Find the Absolute Value Error

workedExample.label: Student thinking
workedExample.work: The number is -6, and absolute value makes it the opposite

workedExample.label: Student answer
workedExample.work: |-6| = 6, and since we take the opposite, the answer is -6

extending.correctWork: Absolute value gives the DISTANCE from zero, which is always positive or zero. |-6| = 6. The student incorrectly applied 'opposite' a second time.
hints: Absolute value measures distance. Can a distance ever be negative?
The student found 6 first, then incorrectly negated it. Distance from zero is always non-negative.

extending.title: (Lesson 9.3) Find the Comparison Error

workedExample.label: Student thinking
workedExample.work: 8 is bigger than 3, so -8 must be greater than -3

extending.correctWork: With negative numbers, the number closer to zero is GREATER. -3 is closer to zero than -8, so -3 > -8. The student compared the digits without considering that negatives work in the opposite direction.
hints: Plot -3 and -8 on a number line. Which one is farther to the right?
For negatives, closer to zero means greater. -3 is only 3 units from zero, but -8 is 8 units away.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Compare and Order Integers is thinking that a negative number with a bigger digit is the bigger value — for example, believing -15 is greater than -8 because 15 is greater than 8. It's the opposite for negatives: the number farther to the left on the number line (farther from zero) is always the LESSER value, so -15 < -8. Before you submit, check your comparison against the number line, not just the digits.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 9.2) Which integer has an absolute value of 8 and is located to the LEFT of zero on the number line?
exitTicket.explanation: To the left of zero means negative. The integer -8 has an absolute value of 8 because it is 8 units from zero.
choiceFeedback: 8 is to the RIGHT of zero — you need the negative side.
Zero's absolute value is 0, not 8 — find distance 8 left.
Its absolute value is 80, not 8 — check the distance from zero.
hints: Two clues to satisfy: distance from zero = 8, AND the point sits to the LEFT of zero.
Left of zero means negative. So you need the negative number that is exactly 8 units from 0.
